P1.section: FINDINGS > 1. Post-earnings announcement drift — the original effect
P1.text:
**CLAIM:** PEAD is the longest-surviving and best-documented directional anomaly; sorting on standardised unexpected earnings (SUE) historically produced roughly 2% abnormal return over the 60 trading days following an announcement, with drift persisting two to three quarters.
**SOURCE:** Ball & Brown (1968), *Journal of Accounting Research*; Bernard & Thomas (1989), *Journal of Accounting Research* 27, 1–36; reviewed in Josef Fink, "A Review of the Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift," University of Graz Working Paper 2020-04 (Nov 2020), https://static.uni-graz.at/fileadmin/sowi/Working_Paper/2020-04_Fink.pdf — **peer-reviewed originals, working-paper review**
**EVIDENCE STRENGTH:** Strong (for the historical effect)
**HORIZON:** Drift strongest in the first quarter after announcement; persists 2–3 quarters. Fink reports Bernard & Thomas at ~2% over 60 trading days, ~4% per quarter; early long/short estimates reach ~18% annualised.
**DECAY EVIDENCE:** See finding 2 — substantial.
**DATA OBTAINABILITY:** Excellent. SUE from a time-series model of quarterly EPS is computable **entirely from EDGAR XBRL** (`EarningsPerShareDiluted`, quarterly, 8+ quarters history). Analyst-based SUE needs IBES or a vendor. Fink notes analyst-forecast-based surprises produce *larger* drift than time-series surprises — so the free version is the weaker version.
**IMPLICATION FOR THE APP:** The 60-day drift window maps cleanly onto 60–90 DTE contracts. This is the single best horizon fit in the entire literature for this product. The problem is entirely whether it still exists.

---

P2.text:
**CLAIM:** Firm-level negative news predicts lower earnings and a one-day price drift, but the drift is ~3 bp/day and the strategy dies at 9–10 bp round-trip transaction costs.
**SOURCE:** Tetlock, Saar-Tsechansky & Macskassy, "More Than Words: Quantifying Language to Measure Firms' Fundamentals," *Journal of Finance* 63(3), 2008, pp. 1437–1467. [PDF](https://business.columbia.edu/sites/default/files-efs/pubfiles/3096/More_Than_Words_tetlock.pdf). Peer-reviewed. DJNS + WSJ stories on S&P 500 firms, 1980–2004. Negative words predict lower SUE at the 99% level in all six specifications; SUE ~0.255 SD lower across a 4-SD move in negative words; ~half the economic impact of recent returns. Depressed earnings persist ≥4 quarters. DJNS next-day abnormal return −3.2 bp per SD; WSJ insignificant. Delayed reaction is ~17% of total for DJNS, ~7% for WSJ. Long-short alpha 9.2 bp/day (1980–94), 11.8 bp/day (1995–2004), positive in 21 of 25 years. **Profits disappear above ~9–10 bp round-trip costs.** Effect ~5x stronger for stories explicitly about earnings.
**EVIDENCE STRENGTH:** Strong.
**IMPLICATION FOR THE APP:** Two actionable items. (1) **Filter news by topic.** Earnings-related negative news is ~5x more informative than general negative news (−39.8 bp vs −8.6 bp same-day). A product that scores all news equally is diluting its own best signal. (2) The cost threshold — profits vanish at ~10 bp — is a death sentence for options implementation. 10 bp on a $100 stock is $0.10; a typical single-name option spread is 20–80× that in equity-equivalent terms.

P3.section: PART 6 — EARNINGS-CYCLE STRUCTURE AT 42–180 DTE > 6.3 The post-earnings window — positive evidence, in the opposite direction to the brief's hypothesis
P3.grade: Strong for the direction (peer-reviewed, explicit offer/bid execution);
P3.text:
**CLAIM:** Straddles bought *after* earnings announcements earn returns more negative than straddles in
firms with no nearby announcement; straddles bought *before* announcements earn about +5.1%; the
long-short portfolio earns about 14.4% over a one-month holding period; combining the announcement-timing
signal with the historical-minus-implied volatility spread raises the hedge return to 29.2% against 13.7%
for the volatility spread alone; and executed at the offer and sold at the bid the two-way strategy still
returns about 14.9% (HV-IV version) and about 9.4% (prior-month volatility version).

**SOURCE:** Sung Gon Chung & Henock Louis, "Earnings announcements and option returns," *Journal of
Empirical Finance*, 2017, 40: 220–235. DOI: 10.1016/j.jempfin.2016.07.010 **[PR]**
The authors attribute the pattern to traders underestimating volatility before announcements (especially
after calm periods) and overestimating it after announcements (especially after volatile periods), and
suggest recency bias as a mechanism. Their stated conclusion is that **post-announcement options appear
expensive** and pre-announcement options appear cheap. They also note single-factor strategies — the
volatility spread alone or announcement timing alone — shrink to small returns after costs.

**EVIDENCE STRENGTH:** Strong for the direction (peer-reviewed, explicit offer/bid execution);
Moderate for magnitude in a retail context, because the headline figures are long-short and the
cost-surviving versions are two-way strategies combining both legs.

P4.section: PART 5: COMPETITION, CAPACITY, AND WHERE RETAIL EDGE MIGHT EXIST > 5.1 Who is on the other side
P4.grade: Moderate-to-Strong (large, granular, but a working paper with a self-selected sample the authors acknowledge).
P4.text:
**CLAIM:** Retail option trades lose ~0.9% each on average including all costs — but short option positions were the profitable exception.

**SOURCE:** Vincent Bogousslavsky (Boston College) & Dmitriy Muravyev (UIUC), "An Anatomy of Retail Option Trading," working paper 8 Feb 2025. [WP] — https://www.brettonwoodsskiconference.com/uploads/b/f9bfc8b0-0251-11ed-a646-3dea17112d2f/An%20Anatomy%20of%20Retail%20Option%20Trading.pdf

- Average option trade returns **−0.9%** including commissions, fees and spreads; stock trades near zero. Sample ~$15bn in trades.
- Per trader-month: option-only traders lose ~**$547**; stock-only traders earn ~$62 (not significant).
- **0DTE options lose ~4.7% per trade** univariately (2.3–3% worse than other options after controls).
- Index/ETF options ~−3% vs single-stock options ~**+0.15%**.
- **Option purchases lose ~4%. Naked option sales — only ~13% of option trades — earn ~20%.** Trader fixed effects do not explain the buyer/seller gap, so it is not a skill difference.
- **Trade size matters: traders averaging under $200/trade lose ~3.4% per option trade vs ~1.4% for those averaging over $5,000.**
- The average loss (−0.9%) is *smaller* than the typical quoted spread (3.7%), implying retail traders do get fills better than quoted — consistent with limit-order use and with the price improvement above.
- The authors note the sample is trade-journal users and may not represent all retail.

**EVIDENCE STRENGTH:** Moderate-to-Strong (large, granular, but a working paper with a self-selected sample the authors acknowledge).

P5.text:
**CLAIM:** Retail option traders lose 5–9% of their option investment around earnings on average, and 10–14% for high-expected-announcement-volatility events, with aggregate losses ≈$3bn.
**SOURCE:** Tim de Silva, Eric C. So & Kevin Smith, "Losing is Optional: Retail Option Trading and Expected Announcement Volatility," *Review of Finance* 30, 2026, pp. 489–535 (online Oct 2025). https://www.timdesilva.me/files/papers/losing_optional.pdf **[PEER]**
**EVIDENCE STRENGTH:** Strong.
**Details:** Nasdaq and PHLX clientele-split trade data matched to 32,758 US quarterly announcements, 2010–2021. Retail buys ATM calls in the days before high-EAV announcements; media coverage appears to drive the attention. Market makers absorb the demand; retail purchases raise option-implied variances by **~40%** for top-quintile retail buying. Three loss channels: (1) options overpriced relative to subsequent realized vol — straddles underperform by **~11%** on high-EAV announcement days vs low-EAV and a further **~9%** over the next 10 days, with no reversal; (2) wide pre-announcement spreads costing **~9%** extra on a half-spread assumption; (3) slow closing of losers consistent with the disposition effect. Retail option dollar volume rose from ~$20bn (2010) to ~$240bn (2020). The authors attribute the behaviour to behavioural error rather than hedging, lottery preference, or private information. Transaction-cost estimates assume hold-to-maturity and half-spread, so they are **lower bounds**.
**IMPLICATION FOR THE APP:** Devastating and specific. "News catalyst" is one of the app's four named selection inputs, and the single best-documented systematic retail loss in the options literature is *buying options into a known catalyst*. Retail demand itself inflates the IV by ~40%, and the loss is three-part: overpricing, spread, and failure to exit. If the app ranks contracts higher because an earnings catalyst is approaching, it is mechanically steering users into the configuration with the largest measured retail loss in the literature. The defensible version of a catalyst input is **negative-signed for long premium** and accompanied by an IV-crush warning.

P6.section: PART 1 — IS THERE A HARVESTABLE VARIANCE RISK PREMIUM IN SINGLE NAMES AT ALL? > 1.4 Does it survive single-name transaction costs? — the decisive evidence
P6.grade: Strong. Peer-reviewed, RFS, largest and most recent sample with explicit cost
P6.text:
**CLAIM:** The best modern machine-learning cross-section of equity option returns earns 2.63%/month
gross but 1.33% at a 15% effective spread and 0.47% at 25%, and **long-dated options (over 90 days)
become insignificant or negative at a 25% effective spread while short-dated ones (≤90 days) survive.**

**SOURCE:** Turan G. Bali, Heiner Beckmeyer, Mathis Moerke & Florian Weigert, "Option Return
Predictability with Machine Learning and Big Data," *Review of Financial Studies*, 2023 (36: 3548–3602);
CFR Working Paper 21-08. **[PR]**
https://academic.oup.com/rfs/article/36/9/3548/7056660
Sample: OptionMetrics, Jan 1996 – Dec 2020; 4,932,372 options on 7,046 underlyings; 12,129,844
option-month observations; out-of-sample 2003–2020. Nonlinear ensemble H-L Sharpe 2.06 gross,
1.17 at 15%, 0.43 at 25%. At 25% the strategy is zero or slightly negative in 2016–2019. Short-term ATM
options have the highest risk-adjusted return (Sharpe 1.34) at 25%. Sample covers about 83% of total US
equity market capitalisation with an average size percentile of 72.

**EVIDENCE STRENGTH:** Strong. Peer-reviewed, RFS, largest and most recent sample with explicit cost
grids.

**IMPLICATION FOR THE BUILD:** Two consequences, both uncomfortable for the brief's stated horizon.
First, **the maturity evidence cuts against the long end of the 42–180 DTE target range.** The only
peer-reviewed study that splits option-return predictability by maturity and nets out costs finds the
over-90-day bucket does not survive a 25% effective spread. The 42–90 DTE sub-band is materially better
supported by evidence than 90–180 DTE, and the build should either concentrate there or explicitly
acknowledge that the 90–180 band is an evidence-free extrapolation. Second, the strategy was flat to
negative in 2016–2019 at 25% costs — the decay concern is live in single names even without a formal
break test.

---

depends_on.why: It is the only claim, and the only finding that carries a direction. Without the earnings miss nothing points to a lower close; every other recorded finding is context with no direction.

checks_that_are_one_problem.note: Both describe the same thin base. The thesis rests on a single finding, and that finding is graded moderate rather than primary-source.
Both come from the breakeven sitting about 2.9% below spot. A modest decline is not enough to profit, so the historical chance of profit falls well below the chance of a lower close.

critic.case_for: Amazon missed its quarterly earnings estimate by about four percent, and revenue also came in slightly short. Long-documented research finds that prices tend to drift in the direction of an earnings surprise for weeks to quarters afterward. The miss came alongside a large cash outflow and plans for heavier spending and more borrowing, which could keep sentiment under pressure through the 30-day window.

priced_in.reading: Since the miss became public the stock has risen 1.2%, about 0.13 of a typical realized move. The figure shows no downward reaction to the miss so far. It is too small to read as a decisive rejection of the miss, but it does not show the drift the claim relies on.

critic.case_against: Amazon closed lower in only about 41% of past 30-day periods, so a decline is the less common outcome. The stock has edged up since the miss instead of drifting down. The drift effect has decayed substantially. Its free, estimate-based version is the weaker one, and news-driven drift is tiny and vanishes after trading costs. The view rests on one moderate finding, and a Fed decision plus active volatility sit inside the window.

loss_paths.title: Decline too small
loss_paths.text: The spread needs Amazon below $252.65 at expiration. Even when the stock closed lower, this structure was profitable in only 70.1% of periods, so a mild decline still loses.

loss_paths.title: Fed day swing upward
loss_paths.text: The 9 December rate decision falls inside the holding period while volatility runs at 1.41 times its typical level. A rally on that event could carry the stock away from the spread.

loss_paths.title: Costs eat the edge
loss_paths.text: Estimated slippage is $30, about 4% of the maximum loss, and closing early costs about the same again. The retail research finds that bought options lose on average after costs.

missing.why_it_matters: Without estimate revisions, it cannot be seen whether analysts have already cut forecasts since the miss, which would bear on further drift.
Only annual consensus is available, so the size and reliability of the quarterly surprise cannot be checked against a quarterly benchmark.

dispositions.reason: The miss is recorded, but the evidence is moderate and stands alone. The revenue shortfall is only 0.1%, and the price has risen slightly since the report. The claim supports a reported miss, not a demonstrated downward drift.

objections.title: The whole view rests on one moderate finding.
objections.text: No second independent finding supports a lower close, and the one finding that does is not graded as primary-source evidence.

objections.title: The market has not moved down on the miss.
objections.text: The stock is up slightly since the report, so the drift the thesis needs has not appeared in the three weeks since.

objections.title: A lower close runs against the base rate.
objections.text: Historically, lower closes over 30 days occurred in about 41% of periods, and the historical chance of profit for this spread is 26.6% against 41.5% implied by the market.

objections.title: A better-fitting candidate was passed over.
objections.text: The best-fit candidate was profitable in every period where the thesis held, against 70.1% for the selected spread.

objections.title: News and drift effects are small after costs.
objections.text: The research shows news-driven drift disappears at modest trading costs and that bought options lose on average for retail traders.
